title: The rise of tokenised money market funds (BIS Bulletin No 115)
summary: BIS staff describe how tokenised money market funds work, trace their growth since 2023 and show where holdings sit. The funds invest mainly in short-dated US government paper and repo, and a handful of wallets, often DeFi protocols, hold most tokens. The authors flag liquidity mismatch, concentration and AML/CFT risks that could echo those of stablecoins and ordinary money funds.

title: Tokenisation of government bonds: assessment and roadmap (BIS Bulletin No 107)
summary: BIS staff build a dataset of tokenised bonds and compare them with ordinary bonds from the same issuer, currency and coupon type. They find tighter bid-ask spreads, similar issuance costs and much lower minimum tickets for the tokenised versions, while stressing the sample is small. Hong Kong SAR is named among sovereign issuers, and the paper argues legal and regulatory uncertainty, not cost, is the main brake.

Its member survey found almost no commercial-scale use, and it sets bond, repo and money fund activity against the size of the traditional markets. It also collects third-party growth forecasts, noting they differ widely and are not endorsed.

It stresses that reliable market-size data do not exist because definitions and models vary and disclosure is thin. It cites only a few indicative numbers for tokens on public chains.

title: Holdings of Cryptocurrencies (IAS 38 Intangible Assets) - agenda decision, June 2019
summary: The Committee explained how existing IFRS Standards apply to holdings of unbacked cryptocurrencies that create no contract with any issuer. Such a holding is not cash and not a financial asset, but it is an intangible asset. It falls under IAS 2 Inventories when the entity holds it to sell as part of normal business (with fair value less costs to sell available to commodity broker-traders), and under IAS 38 otherwise. It lists the disclosures that follow.

rules.point: Scope: a cryptocurrency here means a crypto asset on a distributed ledger, secured by cryptography, issued by no authority or other party, and giving no contract with another party.
A holding of such a cryptocurrency is an intangible asset because it can be separated and sold, and carries no right to a fixed or determinable number of currency units.
It is not a financial asset under IAS 32 and is not cash, because no cryptocurrency is used widely enough as a medium of exchange and pricing unit.
IAS 2 applies when the entity holds the coins to sell in its normal business; broker-traders consider IAS 2 paragraph 3(b) fair value less costs to sell; otherwise IAS 38 applies.
Disclosures: IAS 2 or IAS 38 disclosures, IFRS 13 where fair value is used, IAS 1 judgements, and IAS 10 material non-adjusting events such as later value swings.

methodology_note: Agenda decision of the IFRS Interpretations Committee; explains existing requirements rather than adding new ones. Treated as international_official because the IFRS Foundation is the global standard setter (it is not a regulator). HKFRS mirrors IFRS, so the analysis is directly relevant in Hong Kong.
caveats: Covers only unbacked cryptocurrencies; stablecoins with redemption rights and tokenised securities may be financial assets and need separate analysis. Does not address issuers, custodians, or client assets held by a bank.

summary: VARA's core rules for virtual assets in Dubai (all zones except the DIFC). Schedule 1 lists the licensable activities: advisory, broker-dealer, custody, exchange, lending and borrowing, management and investment, transfer and settlement, and Category 1 issuance. Activities tied to a UAE central bank digital currency stay with the Central Bank of the UAE (CBUAE). This version is dated 19 May 2025; VARA's rulebook site shows it as effective from 19 June 2025.

rules.point: No firm may conduct a VA activity by way of business in Dubai unless VARA has licensed it for that activity, it is an employee of a licensee, or it is an Exempt Entity.
A separate licence is needed for each VA activity a firm will carry on in the Emirate.
Exempt Entities are federal or Dubai government bodies and their public or non-profit entities. They still need VARA's no-objection before starting VA activity. The definition does not list banks.

Issuing anonymity-enhanced cryptocurrencies, and any VA activity involving them, is banned in the Emirate.

Its main themes are asset segregation, a separate legal entity for custody, wallet and key controls, client agreements, monthly statements and audit trails.

rules.point: Assets held in custody are not the custodian's own assets or deposit-type liabilities.
Rehypothecating custodied assets is banned, even if the client consents. Custodians must not ask clients for such consent.
Each client's assets must sit in separate wallets that hold only that client's assets.
The custodian must be a separate legal entity from group companies that run other VA activities. A narrow exception allows it to add transfer and settlement services.
The split between hot, cold and warm storage should rest on a risk-based analysis. Transfer mechanisms between wallet types are subject to independent third-party audit.
Key and seed backups must be kept apart from the primary keys. Mnemonic seed phrases must be split into at least two parts.
Clients get a statement at least monthly, and on request. A transaction audit trail is kept for at least eight years.

methodology_note: Binding VARA rulebook, captured from the official rulebook site.
caveats: Dubai (excluding DIFC) only. The rulebook also has parts on staking from custody and on collateral wallets, which are not summarised here.

title: Exchange Services Rulebook
summary: This rulebook sets extra rules for VARA-licensed exchanges. It covers board and disclosure requirements, a participant code of conduct, market surveillance, system resilience and settlement timing. Separate parts deal with margin trading and exchange-traded derivatives (ETDs), including leverage limits for retail investors and insurance funds. This is the 31 March 2026 version.

rules.point: Exchanges must publish and enforce a code of conduct for trading participants, with a range of disciplinary powers.
Exchanges must share surveillance information with VARA and report suspected market abuse. Their fee structures must not reward disruptive order behaviour.
Final settlement is due within 24 hours of execution, subject to factors outside the exchange's control.
Firms offering ETDs must keep an insurance fund, unless VARA agrees otherwise.

figures.metric: Maximum leverage for retail investors on exchange-traded derivatives
figures.definition: Retail cap that follows from a minimum initial margin of 20%
figures.note: VARA expects higher margin where 5:1 is unsuitable for a client or product.

figures.definition: Time from execution to final settlement of a VA trade on the venue

methodology_note: Binding VARA rulebook, captured from the official rulebook site.
caveats: Dubai (excluding DIFC) only. Hong Kong treats virtual asset derivatives differently, so do not compare them directly without checking the Hong Kong position.

title: Broker-Dealer Services Rulebook
summary: This rulebook applies to VASPs licensed by VARA for Broker-Dealer Services. That activity covers arranging, dealing as principal, market making and placement or distribution for issuers. The rulebook sets a best-execution duty, conditions for principal dealing, a route for adding advisory services, margin trading rules and duties for Licensed Distribution Services.

rules.point: Broker-dealers must use reasonable diligence to get the best price for clients in current market conditions, taking account of costs, speed, likelihood of execution and settlement, and order size. A narrow carve-out covers some quote requests from other VASPs and professional clients.
Dealing as principal, including riskless principal, is allowed but subject to best execution. Client money and client VAs may not be used except as the client-asset rules permit.
A broker-dealer may also give advice if it meets the extra capital requirements and follows the Advisory Services Rulebook.

A firm distributing VAs for issuers is responsible for the quality of those issuers and assets. This includes consumer protection, FATF and sanctions compliance, and fair markets. VARA can order distribution suspended or stopped.

methodology_note: Binding VARA rulebook, captured from the official rulebook site.
caveats: Dubai (excluding DIFC) only.

title: Virtual Asset Issuance Rulebook
summary: This rulebook sorts VA issuance in Dubai into three groups. Category 1 needs a VARA licence and covers fiat-referenced VAs (FRVAs, i.e. stablecoins) and asset-referenced VAs. Category 2 needs no licence but must be distributed through a licensed distributor. Exempt VAs have no prior requirement. Annex 1 sets the FRVA rules: full reserve backing, redemption at par, monthly independent audits and capital. Stablecoins that reference the UAE dirham (AED) are excluded and remain with the CBUAE.

rules.point: Issuing an FRVA or an asset-referenced VA is a Category 1 activity that needs a VARA licence. Other issuances need no licence but must be placed through a licensed distributor.
VARA will not approve a stablecoin that tracks the AED under these rules. Such tokens fall solely under CBUAE regulation.
rules.locator: Schedule 2 'FRVA', pp.23-24; Annex 1 Part I.B.4, p.30

rules.point: FRVAs must be backed at all times by reserve assets worth at least 100% of the tokens in circulation.

Reserves must be in the reference currency. Eligible assets are cash or cash equivalents, government or central bank debt with 90 days or less to maturity, repos of 7 days or less backed by that debt, and short-term government money market funds.
Reserves must be kept with suitably licensed firms, legally segregated from the issuer's own assets and protected from creditors. They must not be rehypothecated or pledged.
Holders have a legally enforceable right to redeem at par. Redemptions must be completed within one working day and without fees.
An independent audit of tokens in circulation and reserve composition is needed every month. Marketing must say the tokens are not covered by deposit guarantee or investor protection schemes.
rules.locator: Annex 1 Part III.D.1 and III.E.2, p.37

title: Market Conduct Rulebook
summary: This rulebook applies to all VARA licensees. It covers marketing, client agreements, complaints, investor classification, public disclosures, insider lists and own-account trading. Investors are sorted into Retail, Qualified and Institutional, and a licence may limit which types a VASP can serve. VASPs are generally barred from actively investing their own or their group's portfolio.

rules.point: VASPs may serve only the investor types VARA permits, within the limits in the rules, their licence conditions and any other VARA conditions.

An Institutional Investor includes any entity regulated by a competent financial regulator (the CBUAE among others), any VASP, central-bank-type institutions, and some governments and multilateral bodies.

VASPs must publish their licence number, licensed activities and responsible individuals, plus a risk statement. The statement must cover loss of value, irreversible transfers, illiquidity and fraud or hacking.
VASPs may not actively invest their own or their group's portfolio. Prudent treasury and liquid-asset management is allowed if records are kept for eight years.

figures.definition: Minimum net assets for an individual or entity to count as a Qualified Investor. The main home is excluded, and only half the value of VAs counts.
Annual income that lets an individual with relevant knowledge qualify instead of meeting the net-asset test

methodology_note: Binding VARA rulebook, captured from the official rulebook site.
caveats: Dubai (excluding DIFC) only. Retail access depends on each licence's conditions, which this rulebook does not list.

title: Compliance and Risk Management Rulebook
summary: This rulebook applies to all VARA licensees. It covers compliance management, AML/CFT including the FATF Travel Rule, client money and client VA rules. Client fiat money must be held in 'Client Account' accounts at third-party banks outside the VASP's group, and money for UAE clients must be at UAE banks. Client VAs must be kept apart from the VASP's own assets and reconciled daily.

rules.point: Client money must be held in a designated client account. It is not the VASP's property and stays outside its estate on insolvency.

Client money must reach a client account within one calendar day. Money for UAE clients must be held at banks in the UAE. Money for non-UAE clients may start at a foreign bank but must be moved to UAE banks, with the move started within 24 hours.
Client accounts may only be kept at deposit-taking banks that are properly authorised and not in the VASP's group.
Client VAs must be kept in wallets separate from the VASP's own assets and held one-to-one. Rehypothecation needs the client's explicit prior consent and the right licence.
Proceeds such as airdrops and staking gains go to the client unless agreed otherwise. VASPs must meet VARA's proof-of-reserves requirements and reconcile client VA balances daily.

methodology_note: Binding VARA rulebook, captured from the official rulebook site.
caveats: Dubai (excluding DIFC) only. The Custody Services Rulebook takes precedence for licensed custodians where the two conflict.

title: MAS Finalises Stablecoin Regulatory Framework
summary: MAS's finalised rules for regulating single-currency stablecoins (SCS) that are pegged to the Singapore dollar or a G10 currency and issued in Singapore. Issuers meeting the framework's reserve, capital, redemption and disclosure requirements can apply to have their token recognised and labelled an 'MAS-regulated stablecoin'; misusing that label can bring penalties. The framework followed an October 2022 public consultation and took the feedback received into account.

rules.point: SCS issuers must hold reserve assets that meet MAS requirements on composition, valuation, custody and audit, so as to give users confidence that the coin's value will hold steady.
SCS issuers are required to keep a floor of capital and liquid holdings on hand, to lower the chance of going insolvent and let the business be wound down in an orderly way if that happens.
SCS issuers must give holders back the par value within the stated deadline after a redemption request.
SCS issuers must tell users how the token's value is kept stable, what rights holders have, and the results of reserve-asset audits.

Only issuers meeting every requirement of the framework may apply for their stablecoin to be labelled an 'MAS-regulated stablecoin'. Falsely using that label can lead to financial penalties, imprisonment for an individual, or a listing on MAS's Investor Alert List.

figures.definition: Longest period an issuer may take to hand a holder the par value after that holder asks to redeem

methodology_note: Official MAS media release, captured from mas.gov.sg.
caveats: Covers only single-currency stablecoins pegged to SGD or a G10 currency and issued in Singapore; other tokens stay under MAS's separate digital payment token regime. A later legislative-amendment consultation, referenced in a related-news link on the same page, was not captured here.

title: Guidelines on Consumer Protection Measures by Digital Payment Token Service Providers [PS-G03]
summary: MAS guidance under the Payment Services Act on how a digital payment token (DPT) service provider should look after customers' assets. A provider is expected to keep customer holdings apart from its own, in a trust account it runs itself or through an outside party it has vetted. The guidance also covers risk controls, a cold-storage minimum, conflict-of-interest handling and where the staff who move customer assets should be based.

rules.point: A provider is expected to keep customer assets in a trust account kept separate from its own assets, whether it runs that account itself or through an outside safeguarding person.

Before placing assets with an outside safeguarding person, a provider should weigh that party's legal protections, financial standing, regulatory status, and whether spreading assets across more than one safeguarding person would help.

Providers are expected to put controls in place so that no single staff member can authorise and carry out a transfer of customer assets alone, and to control transfers between their own storage systems.
Staff and senior managers who control customer-asset movements should be based in Singapore, so they can help return those assets if MAS or a court orders it.

figures.metric: Minimum share of customer assets kept in cold storage
figures.definition: Smallest proportion of customer assets deposited in trust accounts that must sit at all times in wallets cut off from the internet and other wireless links
figures.note: Providers are expected to revisit this periodically and hold more than the floor where their risk profile calls for it.

methodology_note: Binding MAS guideline issued under section 101 of the Payment Services Act 2019. Captured as the PDF linked from MAS's guidelines page; the PDF itself is dated 2 April 2024 and states it takes effect on 4 October 2024, while MAS's guidelines page shows the current version as last revised on 19 September 2024.
caveats: A guideline, not a statute: MAS supervises against the spirit of the document rather than applying it as a fixed rule with set sanctions. Earlier amendment notes listed on MAS's guidelines landing page were not separately captured.

title: MAS Clarifies Regulatory Regime for Digital Token Service Providers
summary: MAS media release narrowing the scope of its Digital Token Service Provider (DTSP) regime, which sits within the Financial Services and Markets Act passed in 2022, following its 30 May 2025 response to consultation feedback. From 30 June 2025 a licence is needed only by firms serving customers solely outside Singapore; MAS says it expects to grant very few such licences given the money-laundering risk and the limits on its ability to supervise overseas-only business. Firms already serving Singapore customers keep their existing status under other Acts.

rules.point: From 30 June 2025, a DTSP providing digital-payment-token or capital-markets-token services solely to customers outside Singapore needs a licence.

MAS has set a high bar for that licence and says it will generally decline to grant one, pointing to higher money-laundering risk and its limited ability to oversee firms whose regulated activity sits entirely offshore.

A firm already serving customers in Singapore stays regulated as before, under the Payment Services Act 2019, the Securities and Futures Act 2001 or the Financial Advisers Act 2001, and may keep serving overseas customers alongside its Singapore ones without extra impact.
A provider dealing only in tokens used for utility or governance purposes falls outside the DTSP licensing regime altogether.

A DTSP that today serves only customers outside Singapore must wind that activity down once the regime starts on 30 June 2025. MAS says it has found only a handful of such firms and has already contacted them.

methodology_note: Official MAS media release, captured from mas.gov.sg.
caveats: Covers the announcement text only; the Financial Services and Markets Act 2022 provisions, regulations and notices referenced in its Annex were not separately captured.

title: Project Guardian (Guardian) overview
summary: MAS's overview of Guardian (originally launched as Project Guardian), a cross-border sandbox pairing regulators, central banks and financial firms to trial asset tokenisation in funds, fixed income and foreign exchange. Its Policymaker Group sits MAS alongside other regulators, including the UK's FCA, Japan's FSA, the IMF and the World Bank; its Industry Group runs named workstreams with banks, asset managers, custodians and market bodies. A linked grant scheme funds digital bond issuance in Singapore.

rules.point: The Policymaker Group brings MAS together with other regulators and central banks, among them the UK Financial Conduct Authority, Japan's Financial Services Agency, the IMF, the World Bank, Banque de France, Deutsche Bundesbank and Swiss FINMA, to work on common standards and cross-border interoperability for digital assets.
Named firms lead each Industry Group workstream: Schroders for Asset and Wealth Management, ICMA for Fixed Income, and Ant Group together with ISDA for Foreign Exchange.
A Global-Asia Digital Grant scheme was set up to help fund the issuance of digital bonds in Singapore, to encourage wider take-up of digital bonds in the market.

methodology_note: Live MAS scheme page, captured on the capture date; the page header itself shows a Published Date of 12 November 2025.
caveats: A point-in-time snapshot: the membership list and the set of linked publications change as the initiative develops. The page now labels the initiative simply 'Guardian', though it remains widely known by its original name, Project Guardian.
